messages.content: You write the short explanations that first-year programming students in India type when a C quiz asks them "Why did you choose that answer?". Reply with a JSON object only.

A student was shown this C code and question.

Code:
int sd(int n) { if (n < 10) return n; sd(n / 10); return n % 10; }

Question: What is sd(123)?
The student answered: 6

The student holds this wrong belief and does not know it is wrong: The recursive call's result is combined automatically

Write 5 different explanations this student might type for why they chose that answer.
Voice: long-winded, walks through the steps one by one, 20 to 35 words.

Rules:
- Each one must show the student's reasoning, not just repeat the answer.
- Write as the student, in the first person or with no subject. Do not judge the answer or say it is wrong.
- Do not name the idea as a rule and do not use textbook terms for the mistake.
- Make the 5 explanations differ in wording and in which part of the code they point at.

Return JSON: {"sentences": ["...", "..."]}

content: {"sentences": ["First sd(123) is not less than ten, so call sd(12), which calls sd(1), and when it returns one, that result gets combined with each remainder somehow.", "Working down: sd(123) goes to sd(12), then sd(1) gives back 1, so returning upward the 2 and 3 remainders add into that result.", "Since sd(1) returns 1, and then sd(12) gives 2, and sd(123) gives 3, the function naturally gathers all these returned digits into one total.", "The base case returns 1, then as the calls finish, the 2 from n percent 10 and the 3 from the outer call get added to it automatically.", "Tracing it, sd(123) drops to sd(12), drops to sd(1) which is 1, and then coming back up the 2 and 3 just accumulate into that value."]}

sentences: First sd(123) is not less than ten, so call sd(12), which calls sd(1), and when it returns one, that result gets combined with each remainder somehow.
Working down: sd(123) goes to sd(12), then sd(1) gives back 1, so returning upward the 2 and 3 remainders add into that result.
Since sd(1) returns 1, and then sd(12) gives 2, and sd(123) gives 3, the function naturally gathers all these returned digits into one total.
The base case returns 1, then as the calls finish, the 2 from n percent 10 and the 3 from the outer call get added to it automatically.
Tracing it, sd(123) drops to sd(12), drops to sd(1) which is 1, and then coming back up the 2 and 3 just accumulate into that value.
